title: Chasing New AI Tools Is Killing My Passion
author: Evans, Ethan et al.
source: Level Up with Ethan Evans (Substack), September 15, 2026
summary: Executive coach Ethan Evans answers a mid-career engineer's email describing AI-tool fatigue and 'zero layoff immunity' by arguing the fix isn't to chase tools faster but to change the underlying question from 'how do I keep up' to 'how do I leverage what AI can't replicate.' He argues relational and human skills, building rapport, explaining technical work to non-technical stakeholders, executive presence, remain AI's weak points and are exactly what senior professionals should invest in making visible. Evans generalizes two lessons: reframing a stuck problem by changing the question, and treating 'showcasing your ability' as a distinct skill from having the ability in the first place.
points: Reframes AI-tool anxiety from 'how do I keep up' to 'how do I leverage what AI can't replicate.'
Argues relational and human skills (rapport, empathy, executive presence) remain AI's weak points and are worth deliberate investment.
Introduces 'change the question' as a general technique for escaping unproductive problem framings.
Distinguishes having expertise from being skilled at making that expertise visible to others.
quotes: The current pace of AI integration in tech feels like a perpetual rat race of tool-chasing with zero layoff-immunity, and it's draining the passion that brought me into this field.
The wrong answer is to chase harder and faster; that will just increase your burnout. Instead, we have to develop a new strategy.
Right now, AI is still weak in terms of relational or human skills. It cannot shake a hand, look you in the eye, or empathize with you when there is a technical problem or system outage.
Being good at something (architecture, strategy, marketing, etc.) is different than showing that you are good at that thing.

In short, the solution to tool chasing is to stop doing it and do something more valuable instead: look for places to showcase your architectural ability and develop every skill necessary to do that, including public speaking, executive presence, and emotional intelligence.
